Approach 1: Latent Self-Correction, From Detection to Correction

A complete account of the Approach 1 work on Qwen3-VL-2B: what was built, why each step was taken, and what every experiment showed. Written for the mid-point report and presentation.

Model: Qwen3-VL-2B (frozen). Datasets: ChartQA, TextVQA, DocVQA, ScienceQA. Every metric is on held-out test splits unless stated. Detailed per-experiment reports are linked in the text and listed in Appendix A.

1. The goal and the road map

Approach 1 asks a vision-language model to notice when its own visual evidence is weak and to act on that before answering. It has two halves.

Detection (the gate). A small network reads the hidden state of the frozen model and outputs the probability that the answer is correct. If this works, the model can be told when to slow down, retry, or hand the question to something else.

Correction. A step that acts on answers the gate flags. Everything in Sections 3 to 11 builds and tests the gate. Section 12 reports the first experiments on acting on it.

Terms used throughoutThe answer-token probability is the untrained baseline: the probability the model itself gave its answer tokens. A linear probe is a trained head with no hidden layer. A head is any small trained network that reads the frozen hidden states. AUROC is the chance that a randomly chosen correct answer gets a higher score than a randomly chosen wrong one.

2. Foundations: what is measured and how

2.1 The model and what is cached

The vision-language model is Qwen3-VL-2B, kept frozen for the whole project. It answers every question once. For each question the last-layer hidden state of the last token is cached in three situations, so that all later experiments reuse them and never run the large model again.

  • Prompt state \(h_q\): the image and the question, ending at the generation prompt. It exists before any answer does.
  • Answer state \(h_a\): the image, the question, and the model's own answer appended. It describes a specific candidate answer.
  • Reference state \(h_{ref}\): the same, with the correct reference answer appended. Used only as training supervision.

Each state is a vector of size \(d = 2048\). Caching is what makes the experiments cheap. Extracting the states of one dataset split takes up to an hour and a half on one GPU (82 minutes for the 28,299 ChartQA training questions with a corrupted image), but a whole pooled sweep of head fits on the cached states takes 3 to 12 minutes per head kind. The price is that nothing the head learns can change what the model sees or says.

2.2 What counts as a correct answer

Each dataset has its own rule, converted to one binary label \(y \in \{0,1\}\). Correctness is judged by the dataset's official scoring, not by exact string match, because exact match would call a right answer wrong whenever formatting differs.

DatasetTrainValidationTestBase accuracy, trainBase accuracy, testCorrect means
ChartQA28,2991,9202,50078.5%75.8%Relaxed accuracy (5% for numbers)
TextVQA8,0001,5002,50082.3%81.0%VQA soft accuracy at least 0.5
DocVQA8,0001,5002,50093.2%87.0%ANLS at least 0.9
ScienceQA6,2181,5002,01786.5%86.7%Option letter matches

ChartQA uses relaxed accuracy (a numeric answer within 5% of the reference). TextVQA uses the VQA soft accuracy over ten human answers, correct at 0.5 or more. DocVQA uses ANLS, correct at 0.9 or more. ScienceQA uses the option letter. Splits are grouped by image or document so that no image appears in two splits, and the validation and test splits of TextVQA and DocVQA are carved out of the official validation split because the official test answers are hidden.

2.3 Metrics

The head outputs a score \(s\) and the probability \(p = \sigma(s / T)\), where \(\sigma\) is the logistic function and \(T\) is a temperature fitted once on the validation split by minimizing the cross-entropy (temperature scaling, Guo et al. 2017). The test split is used only for the final numbers.

  • Correctness AUROC, \(\mathrm{AUROC} = P(s_{\text{correct}} > s_{\text{wrong}})\), the probability that a random correct answer outranks a random wrong one. 0.5 is a coin flip, 1.0 is perfect.
  • Error AUPRC, the area under the precision-recall curve when the wrong answers are the positive class. It measures how well errors are packed at the top of a queue sorted from least to most trusted, which is the view that matters for a gate. Chance equals the error rate.
  • Brier score, \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_i (p_i - y_i)^2\). Lower is better. It rewards being right and being honest about uncertainty.
  • ECE, the expected calibration error, \(\sum_b \frac{|B_b|}{n}\,\bigl|\mathrm{acc}(B_b) - \mathrm{conf}(B_b)\bigr|\) over ten probability bins. Lower is better.
  • Accuracy at coverage: keep the most trusted fraction of answers and report their accuracy. Full coverage equals the base accuracy.
  • Errors captured at a flag rate: flag the lowest-scored fraction of answers and report the share of all errors that fall inside.

2.4 Selection protocol

Every configuration is trained on three seeds. A winner is the configuration with the best mean validation error AUPRC (validation AUROC breaks ties), chosen on the validation split only. Test numbers are read afterwards for the winners. Where a number is shown with a plus-minus sign, it is the standard deviation across seeds. This matters because several differences in this project are a few thousandths of AUROC, which is the size of the seed noise.

3. Stage 1: the model's own confidence

The natural first idea is to use what the model already says about itself. When Qwen3-VL generates an answer of \(m\) tokens, it assigns each token a probability. The geometric mean of those probabilities is a confidence for the whole answer:

\[ c = \exp\!\Bigl(\tfrac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\log p(t_j \mid t_{<j},\ \text{image},\ \text{question})\Bigr) \]

It needs no training and no extra computation. We call it the answer-token probability throughout. Its problem is saturation: modern instruction-tuned models are very sure of their tokens whether or not the answer is right, so the score is exactly 1.0 for most answers and cannot rank them.

DatasetBase accuracyToken probability exactly 1.0AUROCError AUPRCBrierECE
ChartQA75.8%76.6%0.7510.5810.1800.175
TextVQA81.0%79.0%0.7260.4490.1580.152
DocVQA87.0%82.4%0.6850.3330.1140.106
ScienceQA86.7%89.6%0.6540.3230.1160.108
Pooled mixture82.4%81.5%0.7190.4430.1430.136
Why this stage mattersOn the original ChartQA study the score was exactly 1.0 for 1,921 of 2,500 test answers (76.8%), including many wrong ones. Keeping its most confident half of answers raised accuracy only from 75.8% to 92.4%. Across the four datasets the score sits at 1.0 for 77% to 90% of answers, so a threshold on it cannot separate right from wrong. This is the gap the learned heads are built to close, and it is the comparison every later result is measured against.

An answer-length baseline (does a longer answer tend to be wrong?) was also computed as a sanity check on shortcuts. It reaches an AUROC of only 0.52 on the pooled mixture, so the heads below are not simply learning answer length.

4. Stage 2: the original ChartQA study

Question. Before building anything that corrects a model, can the model's internal state tell us when it is about to be wrong? This was first tested on ChartQA alone. The full study is report 01.

4.1 Two heads, two questions

  • The pre-generation head reads \(h_q\) and predicts whether the question will be answered correctly before any answer exists. It measures how hard the question looks to the model.
  • The verifier head reads \(h_a\) and judges one specific generated answer. This is the head a correction step needs, because it scores the candidate itself.

Both are small networks trained on a correct or wrong label, with the language model frozen. The reason for two heads is that they answer different questions at different times: one before the answer (useful to decide whether to generate more carefully), one after (useful to decide whether to keep or revise).

4.2 Architecture and training

The default head is a two-layer network: layer normalization, a linear layer to 512 units, GELU, 10% dropout, one output. It was trained with AdamW (learning rate 0.001, weight decay 0.0001, batch size 512, 20 epochs). The later sweep also tested a plain linear probe \(s = w^{\top}h + b\) and a 256-unit variant. The parameter counts are in Section 5.

4.3 Loss functions of the original study

Both heads use binary cross-entropy plus a ranking loss. The verifier adds a paired loss that uses the reference answer.

\[ L_{\mathrm{BCE}} = -\bigl[y\log\sigma(s) + (1-y)\log(1-\sigma(s))\bigr] \] \[ L_{\mathrm{rank}} = \operatorname*{mean}_{i\in\text{correct},\ j\in\text{wrong}} \operatorname{softplus}\bigl(-(s_i - s_j)\bigr),\qquad \operatorname{softplus}(z)=\log(1+e^{z}) \] \[ L_{\mathrm{pair}} = \operatorname*{mean}_{j\in\text{wrong}} \operatorname{softplus}\bigl(-(s_{\mathrm{ref},j} - s_{\mathrm{cand},j})\bigr) \] \[ L_{\mathrm{pre}} = L_{\mathrm{BCE}} + 0.25\,L_{\mathrm{rank}},\qquad L_{\mathrm{verifier}} = L_{\mathrm{BCE}} + 0.25\,L_{\mathrm{rank}} + 0.25\,L_{\mathrm{pair}} \]

The ranking term compares every correct example with every wrong one in a batch. The paired term compares the model's wrong answer with the correct reference answer for the same image and question, using two teacher-forced passes that differ only in the answer text. The reference is training supervision only: at deployment the verifier sees the image, question and candidate, never the unknown correct answer. The idea was to teach the verifier what a right answer looks like by contrast.

4.4 The sweep

Using cached features, 12 configurations per head, each on three seeds (36 runs per head, 72 in total), were trained: architecture \(\in\) {linear, MLP-256, MLP-512}, learning rate \(\in\) {3e-4, 1e-3}, ranking weight \(\in\) {0, 0.25}, seed \(\in\) {1, 2, 3}. A second sweep added early stopping and five ranking weights for the verifier. The table gives mean validation AUROC of the 72 runs, grouped. The raw runs are in 04_sweep_data/chartqa_original_validation_runs.json.

What the study found(1) The answer-token probability is weak (AUROC 0.750). (2) A small head on frozen states is far better: AUROC 0.89, error AUPRC about 0.74, Brier score 0.178 to 0.11, ECE 0.172 to between 0.03 and 0.04, and accuracy on the most trusted half of answers from 92.4% to about 97%. (3) The linear probe had the highest AUROC (0.895), which says expected difficulty is close to linearly readable from the question state. The early-stopped verifier had the highest error AUPRC (0.738) and is the relevant model for judging a specific answer. (4) The ranking objectives did not help: plain cross-entropy won both heads in the main sweep.

Why these choices were made. Linear probes were included because a linear probe that works is the strongest evidence that the information is already in the hidden state, and not created by the head. The sweep was run on cached features so that the choice of architecture, learning rate and ranking weight rests on 72 fits and not on one lucky run. Selection used validation error AUPRC because for a gate, finding the wrong answers matters more than the average ranking.

5. Head sizes

The size of the heads matters for two reasons: it bounds the cost of using them (they add almost nothing to inference) and it shows that the signal is cheap to read. The counts below are exact, computed from the layer sizes for the 2,048-dimensional hidden state of Qwen3-VL-2B. For scale, the language model has roughly 2 billion parameters, so the largest head here is about 0.1% of it.

5.1 Architectures

  • Linear probe (pre-generation or verifier): \(s = w^{\top}h + b\), with \(d + 1\) parameters.
  • MLP-\(k\) (pre-generation or verifier): LayerNorm \((2d)\), Linear \(d \to k\), GELU, Dropout 0.1, Linear \(k \to 1\). The parameter count is \(2d + dk + k + k + 1\).
  • Unified head: a separate LayerNorm on each half (\(4d\) parameters), then the concatenation \([\,\mathrm{LN}(h_q)\ \|\ \mathrm{LN}(h_a)\ \|\ f\,]\) of size \(2d+1\) (the last entry is a flag), then a linear layer or the same MLP body. The count is \(4d + (2d+1)k + k + k + 1\) for an MLP.

Its 2.11 million parameters are the same as a separate pre-generation head and a verifier of the same width together (2.11 million), so serving one unified head costs about the same as serving the two separate ones.

No single architecture wins everywhere. Linear probes win the pre-generation and unified heads on ChartQA and the verifier on DocVQA, and the other winners use a hidden layer. 6. Stage 3: three more datasets

Why. A result on one dataset can be an accident of that dataset. ChartQA questions are templated, the answers are numbers, and the model's mistakes may have a simple structure. If the heads only worked there, the project would have a ChartQA tool and not a general gate. Three datasets were added, chosen because the model has to do something different in each: read text in a photograph, read a scanned page, and reason over a diagram with a closed answer set. Each has its own correctness rule, grouped splits, and an offline-tested scoring module. Full details are in report 02.

ChartQA

What it asks. Questions about bar, line, and pie charts, written by people and generated by templates. Answers are numbers or short text read or computed from the chart.

Source. HuggingFaceM4/ChartQA. Correct means. Relaxed accuracy: a numeric answer within 5% of the reference counts as correct, text answers need a normalized exact match.

Why it is here. The dataset of the original study, kept as the common reference point.

Splits. Official train, validation, and test splits.

TextVQA

What it asks. Questions that can only be answered by reading text inside a photograph: the brand on a watch, the number on a jersey, what a shirt says. Each question has 10 human answers, which disagree often enough that correctness is a matter of degree.

Source. lmms-lab/textvqa (TextVQA, photographs from Open Images). Correct means. Official VQA soft accuracy over the 10 answers. An answer is labeled correct when the score is 0.5 or more, which needs at least two annotators to agree with it.

Why it is here. Tests a different visual skill (reading small, partial, or stylized text in clutter) and free-form answers with natural annotator disagreement.

Splits. 8,000 training questions sampled from the official train split (34,602). Validation (1,500) and test (2,500) are carved out of the labeled official validation split by image, because official test answers are hidden.

DocVQA

What it asks. Questions about scanned pages from industry documents: letters, forms, reports, tables, handwritten notes. Answers are spans copied from the page. Each question carries a type such as table or list, layout, form, free text, handwritten, or figure or diagram.

Source. HuggingFaceM4/DocumentVQA (DocVQA, UCSF Industry Documents Library). Correct means. ANLS similarity (one minus normalized edit distance to the closest reference). An answer is labeled correct at 0.9 or more, stricter than the 0.5 cutoff used in the official leaderboard.

Why it is here. Dense text at high resolution, long documents, and answers that must match a span exactly, which is very unlike a chart or a photograph.

Splits. 8,000 training questions sampled from the official train split (39,463). Validation (1,500) and test (2,500) are carved out of the labeled official validation split by document, because official test answers are hidden. Page images are capped at 1,536 pixels on the long side.

ScienceQA

What it asks. Grade-school science questions with a picture or diagram, such as maps, genetics crosses, animal classification, experiments, and reading passages. Every question is multiple choice and the model answers with an option letter.

Source. derek-thomas/ScienceQA (image questions only). Correct means. Exact match on the option letter, parsed from the first letter of the reply.

Why it is here. A closed answer set, so the answer itself carries almost no information. It tests whether a correctness head still helps when there is little to read in the answer.

Splits. Official train, validation, and test splits, restricted to questions that have an image.

6.1 Protocol

The same recipe was run per dataset: build the grouped splits, generate the baseline answers, cache the three hidden states, run the separate-head sweep (12 configurations per head, three seeds each) and the unified-head sweep (36 configurations, three seeds, early stopping, maximum 50 epochs, patience 5), and analyze the winners. ChartQA was rerun end to end under this protocol as a pipeline check; it reproduced the original numbers (answer-token probability AUROC 0.751 against 0.750, linear probe 0.895 against 0.895).

Reading the numbersThe learned heads beat the answer-token probability on every dataset and every metric. The gain in AUROC of the unified joint head runs from 0.13 (DocVQA) to 0.27 (ScienceQA). Calibration improves most: ECE falls from the range 0.11 to 0.18 for the probability to between 0.01 and 0.04 for the heads, so the head's number can be read as a probability. The separate verifier and the unified joint head are close everywhere. The pre-generation scores sit lower than the answer-aware ones on TextVQA and DocVQA, where the answer text carries the signal, and close to them on ScienceQA, where the question alone tells the head which topics are hard.

6.3 Using the score as a gate

If a correction step can only act on a fraction of answers, what matters is how many errors the flagged fraction contains. Flagging the 20% of answers with the lowest score:

6.4 Does the head have to be a pair?

Paired bootstrap on the test split (1,000 resamples) gives the difference between the unified head and the separate head of the same kind, as AUROC with a 95% interval. An interval that includes zero means the two are not distinguishable.

DatasetUnified joint minus separate verifierUnified pre-generation minus separate pre-generation
ChartQA+0.0068 (-0.0009 to +0.0147)-0.0003 (-0.0038 to +0.0031)
TextVQA-0.0006 (-0.0111 to +0.0112)-0.0028 (-0.0067 to +0.0011)
DocVQA+0.0238 (+0.0027 to +0.0450)-0.0057 (-0.0110 to -0.0009)
ScienceQA+0.0471 (+0.0339 to +0.0614)+0.0049 (+0.0010 to +0.0087)

In joint mode the unified head is never worse than the separate verifier, and its interval excludes zero in its favor on DocVQA and ScienceQA (on ChartQA and TextVQA the interval includes zero). In pre-generation mode it is within 0.006 AUROC of the separate head: slightly better on ScienceQA, slightly lower on DocVQA, and indistinguishable on the other two. This is why the unified head is kept: it matches two separate heads on the whole and it is one network.

6.5 Calibration

A score is useful as a probability only if it matches how often answers are right. The charts plot, for bins of predicted probability, the observed accuracy of the answers in the bin (bins with fewer than 10 answers are dropped). The dashed diagonal is perfect calibration. The answer-token probability is over-confident: in most bins it sits well below the diagonal, and answers it scores between 0.6 and 0.9 are right only about 30% to 60% of the time. The unified head follows the diagonal closely, which is why its ECE is low.

The caught errors show what the head is picking up: overlong or looping generations (a repeated string on a TextVQA question, a long list of buttons), chart arithmetic written out step by step, and answers that name the wrong option. Two kinds of missed error appear. Some are confident misreads, such as a wrong value read from a chart, which a head that only sees hidden states has no way to check. Others are answers that are right in spirit and marked wrong by the strict label rule ("live" for a question whose reference is "yes", "24 parts" against "24"), so part of the missed-error count reflects label noise and not head failure. The false alarms show the reverse: correct answers in an unusual format ("1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 0" for "1234567890") that the head distrusts.

6.9 A length shortcut check

If wrong answers were simply longer, a head could score well by counting characters. An answer-length score alone (length in characters, shorter answers scored as more likely correct) reaches only the AUROCs below, where 0.5 is chance and the heads reach 0.78 to 0.92, so the heads are not using length as a shortcut. TextVQA is the one dataset where length carries some signal (wrong answers average 13.7 characters against 7.8), and the heads still beat it by more than 0.25 AUROC.

7. Stage 4: the unified head

The idea. Two separate heads need two networks, two trainings and two decisions about which to trust. A single head that reads both states removes that. It also gives a natural way to combine them: the question state \(h_q\) gives the difficulty prior, and the answer state \(h_a\) gives the evidence about this particular answer.

7.1 Design

Each half is normalized separately, so neither dominates by scale. The input is the concatenation and a flag \(f\):

\[ x = \bigl[\ \mathrm{LN}_q(h_q)\ \|\ \mathrm{LN}_a(h_a)\ \|\ f\ \bigr],\qquad s_{\mathrm{joint}} = g(x),\ f=1 \] \[ s_{\mathrm{pre}} = g\bigl(\bigl[\ \mathrm{LN}_q(h_q)\ \|\ \mathbf{0}\ \|\ 0\ \bigr]\bigr) \]

With the answer half zeroed and the flag at 0, the same network scores a question before any answer exists (pre-generation mode). With both halves present it scores a candidate answer (joint mode). This is trained jointly with a loss that keeps both modes useful:

\[ L = L_{\mathrm{BCE}}(s_{\mathrm{joint}}, y) + w_{\mathrm{pre}}\,L_{\mathrm{BCE}}(s_{\mathrm{pre}}, y) + w_{\mathrm{rank}}L_{\mathrm{rank}} + w_{\mathrm{pair}}L_{\mathrm{pair}} \]

The reason for the pre-generation term is that a head trained only on the joint input would learn to rely on the answer half and could be useless when the answer half is empty. The flag and the zeroing teach it a separate, honest mode for the question-only case.

7.2 Results

Test AUROC per dataset, separate heads against the unified head in the same mode.

DatasetSeparate pre-generationUnified, pre-generation modeSeparate verifierUnified, joint mode

FindingsThe unified head's pre-generation mode matches the separate pre-generation head to within 0.007 AUROC on every dataset, and its joint mode matches or beats the separate verifier on all four datasets (the largest gains are on DocVQA and ScienceQA). The pre-generation loss term costs almost nothing: it lifts the question-only mode on every dataset and moves the joint mode by at most 0.006 AUROC on validation. The pairwise reference-answer loss lowered validation AUROC on every dataset and is switched off in all winning configurations. One network therefore does the job of two without a measurable loss.

8. Stage 5: one head for all four datasets

Why. The per-dataset heads show that the signal exists in each dataset. A deployed gate does not know which dataset a question comes from. The pooled experiment asks whether one head, trained on a mix, scores all of them well, and whether it pays a price against heads trained on a single dataset. Details are in report 05.

Setup. The mixture is the union of the four datasets' existing splits: 50,517 training rows, 6,420 validation rows, 9,517 test rows, with an overall base accuracy of 82.4% on the test split. Nothing was resampled, so every test question is one the per-dataset study also scored. One calibration temperature is fitted on the pooled validation split. The sweep has 36 head configurations for the pre-generation head and for the verifier and 72 for the unified head, each on three seeds, covering the old loss (no grounding term) and the new loss.

9. Loss functions

Three loss designs were run on the same heads, features and selection protocol, so differences can be attributed to the loss.

9.1 The old loss

The old loss asks only for the right label on real inputs (Sections 4 and 7): cross-entropy, with a pre-generation term for the unified head. A head trained this way can reach a high AUROC by learning which kinds of questions the model tends to get wrong, without ever using what the image shows. That is useful for ranking, but it is not what a correction step needs, which is a score that reacts when the visual evidence is missing.

9.2 The new loss

The proposed loss has three lines, and each maps to one term:

\[ P_\theta(S_{\mathrm{conf}} \mid h_{\mathrm{answer}}, h_{\mathrm{question}}) \ \to\ L_{\mathrm{cls}}\ (\text{and } L_{\mathrm{pre}}) \] \[ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{contrastive}}(h_{\mathrm{predicted}}, h_{\mathrm{correct}}) \ \to\ L_{\mathrm{pair}} \] \[ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{contrastive}}(h_{\mathrm{clean}}, h_{\mathrm{corrupt}}) \to S_{\mathrm{conf}}\ (\text{visual grounding}) \ \to\ L_{\mathrm{ground}} \]

Written out for a mini-batch:

\[ L = L_{\mathrm{cls}} + w_{\mathrm{pre}}L_{\mathrm{pre}} + w_{\mathrm{pair}}L_{\mathrm{pair}} + \lambda\,L_{\mathrm{ground}} \] \[ L_{\mathrm{ground}} = \operatorname*{mean}_{m\in\text{modes}}\ \operatorname*{mean}_{i\in\text{correct}} \operatorname{softplus}\bigl(\text{margin} - (s_m(x^{\mathrm{clean}}_i) - s_m(x^{\mathrm{corrupt}}_i))\bigr),\qquad \text{margin}=0 \] \[ L_{\mathrm{pair}} = \operatorname*{mean}_{i\in\text{wrong}} \operatorname{softplus}\bigl(-(s(x^{\mathrm{ref}}_i) - s(x^{\mathrm{pred}}_i))\bigr) \]

Here \(x^{\mathrm{clean}}\) is the real image with the question and the model's answer, \(x^{\mathrm{corrupt}}\) is the same question and answer text with a corrupted image, \(x^{\mathrm{ref}}\) appends the correct answer and \(x^{\mathrm{pred}}\) appends the model's own answer. The old loss is the case \(\lambda = 0\). The grounding term is applied only to answers the model got right: for those, the evidence is genuinely in the image, so removing the image should lower the score. For wrong answers there is nothing to ground, so they enter only through the correctness loss. The second line (the pair term) is our reading of the proposal's second contrastive term; an embedding-level contrastive loss would need a change to the head loss and was not tried.

9.3 Corrupting the image: swap and noise

The grounding term needs a corrupted image. Two were built, in this order.

  • Swap. Replace the image with a different example's image from the same split. Simple and strong, but it has a weakness: the corrupted pair is also a mismatched question and image, so a head can satisfy the term by detecting the mismatch, without judging how well the image supports the answer.
  • Noise. Keep the right image and mix Gaussian noise into it, the forward step of a diffusion process (Ho et al. 2020): \(x' = \sqrt{\alpha}\,x + \sqrt{1-\alpha}\,\varepsilon\), \(\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)\), with \(\alpha = 0.15\). The scene is still there but its detail is not, so there is no mismatch to detect. The strength was chosen from a smoke test of 30 examples per dataset, by how far the model's own answer probability falls.

Mask (60% of a 16 by 16 grid blanked) and patch shuffle (a 4 by 4 grid permuted) were also built. They were extracted for the test splits and used only to grade heads on corruptions they never trained on. Everything was run through the same pipeline: a pooled sweep for each corruption, a re-grade of the swap heads under the other corruptions, one sweep per dataset alone for each corruption, and sequential training (Section 10). Details: reports 05 (swap) and 06 (noise).

9.4 How grounding is measured

For each correct test answer, the head scores the pair with the clean image and with the corrupted one. Order accuracy is the share of correct answers whose score falls under corruption (0.5 means no effect, 1.0 means it always falls). It is the number quoted in the results as "the score falls". The untrained answer-token probability can be graded the same way.

On ChartQA, TextVQA and DocVQA the old-loss head already lowers its score on about 0.97 or more of correct answers under noise (all three head kinds), so there is little room and AUROC does not move. ScienceQA is where the term matters: the old loss lowers the score on 0.69 to 0.78 of correct answers under noise across the three head kinds, close to indifferent, and the noise loss raises that to 0.87 to 1.0 (the table shows the unified head: 0.72 to 0.94). ScienceQA questions can often be answered from the text alone, so a score that ignores the image is the expected outcome without the term.

How far to trust the grounding numbersOrder accuracy near 1.0 is partly easy. A noised image moves the hidden state a lot, so a head can learn to lower its score on noisy-looking inputs without checking whether the image supports the answer. The cross-corruption check lowers this worry but does not remove it. A stronger test is a corruption that removes only the evidence for the answer (for example, masking only the region the answer comes from), which was not run. The noise strength was set on a 30-example smoke test and only one strength was trained.

9.9 What the corrupted images look like

The same clean test image, the swapped partner (another example's image from the same split), and the noised version used by the noise loss. The noised image keeps the layout but loses most of the detail, which is why a head cannot satisfy the noise term by detecting a question and image mismatch. Note that for ScienceQA the swapped partner is another map of a similar kind, so the swap is a milder corruption there than on the other datasets, which may be part of why grounding is lowest on ScienceQA with swap.

10. Stage 6: sequential training and forgetting

The question. The mixture trains on all datasets at once, which is the easy case. In practice a head may be trained on dataset A, then updated on B and C. Does it still score A well afterwards? This is catastrophic forgetting, and it decides whether the heads can be extended to new data without retraining from scratch.

10.1 Protocol

One head is trained through the four datasets in a fixed order, continuing from the previous weights, with early stopping on each stage's validation split. After every stage the head is scored on every dataset's test split, giving a stage-by-dataset matrix of AUROC. Three orders (forward, reverse, shuffled) and three seeds are averaged. The head configurations are the winners of the pooled sweeps, so the old and new loss are compared at the settings chosen on validation. Two variants of each loss were run: plain sequential training, and with a replay buffer, which mixes a fixed 10% random sample of every earlier dataset's training rows into each later stage.

Let \(M_{t,d}\) be the AUROC on dataset \(d\) after stage \(t\), \(T\) the number of stages, and \(\tau(d)\) the stage at which \(d\) is trained. The metrics are:

\[ \text{final average}=\tfrac{1}{D}\sum_d M_{T,d},\qquad \text{forgetting}=\tfrac{1}{D-1}\sum_{d\ne \text{last}}\Bigl(\max_{t\ge\tau(d)}M_{t,d}-M_{T,d}\Bigr) \] \[ \text{backward transfer}=\tfrac{1}{D-1}\sum_{d\ne\text{last}}\bigl(M_{T,d}-M_{\tau(d),d}\bigr),\qquad \text{retention}=\tfrac{1}{D}\sum_d\bigl(M_{T,d}-M^{\text{alone}}_{d}\bigr) \]

Retention compares the final head with a head trained on that dataset alone. The last column of the tables is the grounding order accuracy after the final stage, averaged over datasets.

FindingsHeads trained through all four datasets in sequence keep most of what they learned: forgetting is about 0.011 to 0.015 AUROC for the unified head, 0.013 to 0.025 for the pre-generation head, and the answer-conditioned verifier forgets the most (0.032 to 0.046 without replay). A 10% replay buffer cuts the verifier's forgetting to about 0.005 to 0.008 and changes little for the others. The new loss does not change forgetting much for the unified head, and the noise loss is slightly worse than the swap loss without replay on the pre-generation and verifier heads, with replay removing the difference. Grounding is not forgotten: after the last stage the share of correct answers whose score falls is higher with the new loss than with the old loss in every row.

12. Stage 8: using the head to correct answers

The previous sections built the gate. These experiments test whether acting on it helps. All of them use the frozen Qwen3-VL-2B and the exported pooled-mixture unified head (trained_heads/approach1/winners/mixture/unified_new_seed1.pt), on a balanced study set of 100 examples, 25 from each dataset, of the pooled test split. These experiments were pushed to the feature/latent-self-correction branch (commit e6aaa80) and are not on main yet. The code is in prompted_retry.py, online_prompted_retry.py, candidate_reranking.py and deepen_selected_candidate.py, run by run_prompted_retry.sbatch, run_candidate_reranking.sbatch and run_deepen_selected.sbatch, with sampling options added to models/run_inference.py and tests in tests/test_prompted_retry.py. The full report is 07. Accuracy is the dataset's own metric converted to the binary correctness definition used to train the head.

About "chain of thought"The deeper pass (Section 12.4) is the experiment described as chain of thought: after a candidate is chosen, the model is told to think more deeply, re-examine the visual evidence and correct the candidate. It ran on the same 100 examples with a limit of 64 new tokens. The prompt still ends with respond with only the final answer, without explanation, and most of the time the model complied with a short answer. It did not always. In 5 cases (all ChartQA) it wrote out reasoning anyway, such as a list of the chart values or a subtraction, and ran into the 64-token limit before reaching a final answer. In 5 further cases (4 in DocVQA, 1 in TextVQA) it repeated the prompt text instead of answering. So the run mixes direct answers, a few cut-off chains of thought and a few format failures. It is not a controlled chain-of-thought experiment: reasoning was not requested, was not given enough tokens, and no final answer was extracted from it. A proper run (ask for reasoning, allow enough tokens, extract the final answer) has not been done.

12.1 Prompted retry

Idea. The model answers once. A second prompt shows it the previous answer and asks it to inspect the visual evidence again. The head decides when to retry, so the retry's cost and its risk of overturning correct answers are spent only where the gate thinks the first answer is weak. Each policy is evaluated on the same retry outputs, so there is no generation noise between rows. A random 20% control has the same compute as the head-targeted policies.

Your previous answer was: {answer}
Try the question again. Carefully inspect the visual evidence, including labels, values, and spatial relationships. Do not assume the previous answer is correct.
Respond with only the final answer, without explanation.
PolicyAccuracyRetriedFixedBrokenChartQATextVQADocVQAScienceQA
No retry (greedy answer kept)81.0%0+0-056%88%92%88%
Retry every answer78.0%100+4-760%88%88%76%
Retry if head score below 0.578.0%17+2-556%88%92%76%
Retry the 20% with the lowest head score78.0%20+2-556%88%92%76%
Retry the 20% with the lowest answer-token probability76.0%20+1-652%88%88%76%
Retry a random 20% (control)82.0%20+1-056%88%92%92%

This first run began at 81% for the greedy answer. Retrying every answer lowered accuracy to 78%, and head-based targeting also reached 78%, while the random control reached 82%. In this run a single prompted retry is unstable: it fixes some errors but overturns more correct answers, and the head's flagging did not beat random choice.

12.2 Scored retry and reranking

Idea. Instead of trusting the retry, score both the original and the retry with the same head and keep the one with the higher score. Gated variants also require the original to score below 0.5 and optionally require a minimum improvement, so that the retry replaces the original only with good evidence.

PolicyAccuracyRetriedFixedBrokenChartQATextVQADocVQAScienceQA
No retry (greedy answer kept)79.0%0+0-052%84%92%88%
Retry every answer79.0%100+4-460%84%92%80%
Retry if head score below 0.580.0%18+3-256%84%92%88%
Retry the 20% with the lowest head score80.0%20+3-256%84%92%88%
Retry the 20% with the lowest answer-token probability78.0%20+1-252%84%92%84%
Retry a random 20% (control)78.0%20+0-152%84%92%84%
Head reranking: keep the higher-scored of original and retry79.0%4+2-256%84%92%84%
Gated: retry only if original below 0.5 and retry scores higher80.0%3+2-156%84%92%88%
Gated, margin 0.0579.0%2+1-152%84%92%88%
Gated, margin 0.1079.0%0+0-052%84%92%88%
Gated, margin 0.2079.0%0+0-052%84%92%88%
Oracle: use the retry exactly when it fixes an error83.0%4+4-060%84%92%96%

This run was generated independently and its greedy baseline is 79%. Here the head-targeted retries (below 0.5, or the lowest 20%) reached 80% with 3 fixes and 2 breaks, above the random control (78%) and the baseline (79%), and the gated reranking also reached 80% (2 fixes, 1 break). The oracle is 83%. So in this run the head-guided retry is one point better than doing nothing, and in the first run it was three points worse than doing nothing. The two runs differ because of generation and GPU nondeterminism, and the effect in both is within a few questions out of 100, so the honest reading is that a prompted retry does not clearly help, with or without the head. Comparisons are only meaningful within a table.

12.3 Best-of-five candidate selection

Idea. Separate creating candidates from choosing between them. Five answers are sampled at temperature 0.9 and top-p 0.95. The head scores every candidate from its answer-state \(h_a\), and the highest score is selected: \(\hat a = \arg\max_k\, p_\theta(\text{correct} \mid h_q, h_{a_k})\). The comparison methods are the first sample, a majority vote over normalized answer text, the sample with the highest answer-token probability, the greedy baseline, and an oracle that picks a correct candidate whenever one exists (an unattainable upper bound).

Selection methodAccuracy95% intervalChartQATextVQADocVQAScienceQA
Greedy answer78.0%69% to 85%52%84%92%84%
First of five samples80.0%71% to 87%52%88%92%88%
Majority vote of five80.0%71% to 87%52%88%92%88%
Highest answer-token probability78.0%69% to 85%52%84%92%84%
Highest head score81.0%72% to 87%52%92%96%84%
Oracle: any correct candidate85.0%77% to 91%56%92%96%96%
How strong is the evidence?Each study has 100 examples. At that size, 81% accuracy has a 95% interval of about 72% to 87% and 78% has 69% to 85%, so the intervals overlap heavily. Head selection changed the outcome of 5 questions against greedy: it fixed 4 and broke 1. A paired sign test on 4 against 1 gives a two-sided p-value of about 0.38. The direction is encouraging, but the experiment is too small to claim the improvement is real. A run on the full test split is the next step. The candidate-level check is cleaner: over the 500 sampled answers, the head's score has AUROC 0.879 for telling correct from wrong candidates, against 0.813 for the answer-token probability.

Cases where head selection changed the outcome

Every example where the head-selected candidate was right and greedy was wrong, or the reverse. Long ScienceQA contexts are shortened.

ExampleQuestionReferenceGreedy answerHead-selected candidate

Candidate sets contained 1.36 unique answers on average and all five samples agreed on 76% of examples. Head selection improved greedy accuracy by three points and captured three of the seven points between greedy and the oracle. The head selector (81%) scored one point above the majority vote (80%) and three above the answer-token probability (78%). These are small margins on 100 examples. Note that the first sample alone (80%) is already close to the head's choice, so most of the gain over greedy may come from sampling and not from selection; only the larger run can separate the two.

12.4 A deeper pass after selection

Idea. After the head picks a candidate, the model sees that candidate and is asked to think more deeply and correct it. The head then decides whether the deeper answer replaces the candidate.

PolicyAccuracyFixedBrokenChartQATextVQADocVQAScienceQA
Keep the head-selected candidate81.0%+0-052%92%96%84%
Replace with the deeper answer, always73.0%+2-1048%80%76%88%
Keep the higher head score of the two81.0%+0-052%92%96%84%
Deeper answer if its head score is higher81.0%+0-052%92%96%84%
Deeper answer if at least 0.05 higher81.0%+0-052%92%96%84%
Deeper answer if at least 0.10 higher81.0%+0-052%92%96%84%
Deeper answer if at least 0.20 higher81.0%+0-052%92%96%84%
Oracle: deeper answer exactly when it fixes the candidate83.0%+2-052%92%96%92%

Replacing every selected candidate with the deeper answer lowered accuracy from 81% to 73% (2 fixed, 10 broken). Every head-based replacement rule left the answers unchanged: the head never scored the deeper answer high enough to replace the selected candidate. The oracle for this step is 83%, so there is only a small upper bound to gain even with a perfect rule.

Is the drop only a format problem? Partly. Of the 10 answers the deeper pass broke, 5 are format failures: 1 was cut off at the 64-token limit and 4 repeated the prompt instead of answering. The other 5 are real changes of a correct answer to a wrong one, against 2 real fixes. So fixing the format would shrink the loss but would not turn it into a gain on this sample, and a controlled run with a larger token budget and answer extraction is needed before concluding anything about chain of thought.

12.5 What the correction experiments show

Findings(1) The trained head works as a component: loaded from the repository and used to score freshly generated answers, it gives a candidate-level AUROC of 0.879 against 0.813 for the answer-token probability. (2) Asking the same model to retry or think more deeply is unreliable. It fixes some errors and breaks others. With this head as the gate the net effect ranged from -3 to +1 points between runs and policies, and the deeper pass was clearly harmful when applied to everything (-8 points). (3) Generating several candidates and letting the head choose is the most promising direction: 81% against 78% greedy, with an 85% oracle. (4) All of this is on 100 examples, so none of the differences is statistically established. The next step is to rerun best-of-five on the full pooled test split (9,517 questions) and to add a latent correction step that acts on the hidden state directly, which is the part of Approach 1 that has not been started.

13. Engineering and reproducibility

  • Everything runs on the GT ICE cluster with one command per stage. run_qhead_pipeline.sh runs a dataset end to end (splits, baseline, features, sweeps, analysis), run_mixture_pipeline.sh the mixture and swap loss, run_continual_pipeline.sh sequential training, run_corruption_pipeline.sh the noise loss and its cross-corruption checks, and run_export_pipeline.sh saves the trained heads. Each submits Slurm jobs with dependencies.
  • Scripts are checked before long runs. check_scripts.sh validates shell syntax, that every python -m module resolves, and (on the cluster) that the scheduler accepts the resource request. Time limits are realistic on purpose, because the cluster caps the total GPU minutes a user can request.
  • 36 offline tests cover the scoring rules, the splits, the unified head, the corruptions, the old and new loss (including a check that the old loss is reproduced exactly when the new terms are off), the grounding metrics, the mixture builder, sequential training, and that the reports build from the real result schema. They need no GPU or network.
  • Feature caching is what makes the experiments affordable. After one pass of the language model, a pooled sweep (36 or 72 head configurations, three seeds each, on 50,517 training rows) took 3 to 12 minutes per head kind on a single GPU, and a sequential-training run took 1.5 to 3.5 minutes.
  • Layout. models/ (model loading and inference), data/ (dataset acquisition and scoring inputs), experiments/ (training, analysis, reports), slurm/, results/approach1/ (numbered reports and data), trained_heads/, docs/, tests/.

The design note docs/approach1_unified_q_head.md records the dataset choices and the reasons other candidates were rejected.

14. What it all means

14.1 What is established

  • The detection half works. A small head on frozen hidden states predicts whether an answer is correct far better than the model's own token probability, on four different kinds of input (AUROC 0.881 against 0.719 pooled), and the ChartQA result reproduces end to end.
  • The signal is cheap. A linear probe with about 2,000 parameters already captures most of the gain; the largest head has 2.1 million parameters, about 0.1% of the language model.
  • One head is enough. The unified head does the job of two with no measurable loss, and one head trained on a pool of datasets stays within 0.015 AUROC of heads trained on one dataset.
  • Heads can be extended. Training on one dataset after another loses 0.011 to 0.046 AUROC depending on the head and the loss (the verifier forgets most), and a 10% replay buffer removes most of that for the verifier.
  • A grounding term is cheap. It makes the score react to a corrupted image (the share of correct answers whose score falls goes from 0.92 to 0.99 under noise for the unified head) without costing ranking quality, and the effect carries over to corruptions it was not trained on. The pair term, applied alone, costs AUROC.

14.2 What is not established

  • Correction. Nothing yet shows that acting on a flagged answer improves accuracy. The prompted retry and the deeper pass did not help, and best-of-five selection by the head is promising on 100 examples but not statistically established.
  • Grounding is a proxy. "The score falls when the image is corrupted" shows the head reacts to the image, not that it tracks the specific evidence for the answer. Noise is an easy corruption.
  • One model size. Everything is on Qwen3-VL-2B. The 4B check was not run. The exported sequential heads are single seeds.
  • Calibration across datasets. One temperature is fitted on the pooled validation split. Per-dataset calibration was not studied.

14.3 Next steps

  1. Run best-of-five and the retry policies on the full pooled test split with intervals.
  2. Run a controlled chain-of-thought condition: ask for reasoning, allow enough tokens (the deeper pass used 64), extract the final answer, score it with the head, and compare it with the deeper pass.
  3. Build the latent correction step: test-time steering of the hidden state toward a higher head score, evaluated against the prompted baselines above.
  4. A harder grounding test: mask only the region the answer comes from; and a softer correctness label for span answers.
  5. Check the 4B model, and add extra input features to the head (several layers, image tokens).

A.2 Glossary

TermMeaning
Answer-token probabilityThe geometric mean of the probabilities the model gave its own answer tokens. The untrained baseline.
Linear probeA trained head with no hidden layer, \(s = w^{\top}h + b\).
Pre-generation headScores a question before any answer exists, from the prompt state.
Verifier headScores a specific generated answer, from the answer state.
Unified headOne network that reads both states, with a mode that works without the answer.
AUROCProbability that a random correct answer outranks a random wrong one.
Error AUPRCHow well the wrong answers are packed at the top of a queue sorted by trust.
Order accuracy (grounding)Share of correct answers whose score falls when the image is corrupted. 0.5 means no effect.
ForgettingAverage drop from the best score a dataset had after its own stage to its score after the last stage.
ReplayMixing a fixed share of earlier datasets' training rows into each later stage.
OracleAn unattainable upper bound that uses the ground truth to choose.
